classification_signals: The abstract states: 'This article contributes to the development of a theoretical framework to address and explain all human behavior toward or linked with buildings, dwellings and settlements...' and 'This exploratory article aims to reopen debate on this issue through a series of case studies that are both cross-cultural and cross-disciplinary.' (p. 2)

The paper explicitly states its aim: 'This article argues for the configuration of a theory of architecture that can serve as a tool for understanding the nature of all designed, arranged, and/or constructed environments used as human habitats across all cultural contexts.' (p. 2)
It reviews and synthesizes existing theoretical ideas from various scholars (Rapoport, Oliver, Egenter, Hillier, Barker, Wright, Lethaby, Derrida, Shils, Fox, etc.) to build its argument (p. 3-16).

The 'case studies' (e.g., Australian Aboriginal travelers' camp, Maya dwellings) are presented as illustrations of theoretical points, drawing on the authors' and others' prior empirical research, rather than presenting new empirical data collected for this specific publication (e.g., 'recorded in 1991 by Memmott,' p. 7; 'Davidson's findings show,' p. 11).

Section titles like 'ADDRESSING THE ARCHITECT/BUILDER DISTINCTION AND "AUTHORITY"', 'A DYNAMIC DEFINITION OF "TRADITION"', 'SETTINGS AS ARCHITECTURE', 'MEANING AND ARCHITECTURE', 'CHANGING ARCHITECTURAL TRADITIONS', and 'RECONCILING VALUES' indicate a focus on theoretical development and conceptual framing.
title: Exploring a Cross-Cultural Theory of Architecture

findings.antecedent: All human behavior toward or linked with buildings, dwellings and settlements
findings.consequent: A unifying cross-cultural theoretical framework of architecture
findings.quote: This article contributes to the development of a theoretical framework to address and explain all human behavior toward or linked with buildings, dwellings and settlements

findings.consequent: Exclusion of non-Euro-American and indigenous building traditions from universal theory
findings.quote: questioning why the Euro-American concept of architecture... has so far failed to achieve such a position, at times excluding non-Euro-American and indigenous building traditions.

findings.consequent: Proportion designed by professional architects
findings.quote: In 2003 Paul Oliver estimated that there were likely a billion dwellings in the world, and it was unlikely that even 1 percent had been designed by professional architects.

findings.consequent: Diversity, specialization, and heterogeneity, lying closer to high-style on the continuum of building traditions
findings.quote: ...the vernacular is generally characterized by diversity, specialization and heterogeneity, and 'lies closer to high-style on the continuum of building traditions.'

findings.consequent: Marginalization or ignorance by the Architecture discipline
findings.quote: Others' architectures more generally were acknowledged and valued by anthropology and other disciplines, but were usually marginalised or simply ignored by Architecture.

findings.consequent: Need for modernity to understand, respect, and value Others' cultural productions, which embed cross-cultural richness that contributes to universal cultural heritage
findings.quote: [The] theoretical issues raised by Architecture's continuing cultural discrimination provide[s] a context for re-asserting the need for modernity to understand, respect, and value Others' cultural productions.

findings.antecedent: Western tradition's view of vernacular architecture
findings.consequent: Stigma of underdevelopment, poverty, and the past
findings.quote: We share the view of Lindsay Asquith and Marcel Vellinga, who have recently called for the Western tradition to rid itself of the stigma of underdevelopment, poverty, and the past that clings to the idea of vernacular building...

findings.consequent: Cleavage of modest dwellings from palaces/great houses, and humble chapels from cathedrals; high-style buildings preserved by other disciplines like art history ('poor anthropology')
findings.quote: The available literature on vernacular buildings tends to cleave modest dwellings from palaces or 'great houses,' a humble chapel from a cathedral. High-style buildings form the preserve of other disciplines such as art history. For our purposes this is poor anthropology.

findings.consequent: Architecture (defined as 'all that hominids built and build')
findings.quote: Egenter, who (drawing on the work of Yerkes and Yerkes in the 1920s) defined 'architecture as all that hominids built and build.'

findings.consequent: Support for desired behavior/activities
findings.quote: Rapoport's premise to the theory of environment-behavior relations therefore posits that built environments are created to support desired behavior, and that 'activities' can be taken to be specific units of enactments of behavior.

findings.antecedent: Intellectual choice and systematic manipulation of form
findings.consequent: Architecture (defined as successful accomplishment of systematic, abstract, and comparative manipulation of form)
findings.quote: Hillier's theory is that architecture arises from within a process of 'intellectual choice and decision exercised in a field of knowledge of possibility that goes beyond culture into principle.' Thus, a building is architecture when we can observe the successful accomplishment of a systematic, 'abstract and comparative manipulation of form within the general realm of architectural possibility.'

findings.consequent: Dichotomy between 'active' building systems (Euro-American architecture) and 'passive building systems' (cultural template of vernacular design)
findings.quote: This definition also establishes a dichotomy between the 'active' building systems of 'architecture' in the Euro-American sense, and the 'passive building systems' that reproduce a cultural template of vernacular design.

findings.antecedent: Hillier's definition of architecture (confined to spatial configurations)
findings.consequent: Neglect of creative manipulation of materials, construction, structural systems, artifactual configurations, meanings, and behavioral usage
findings.quote: Hillier's persistence in largely confining the definition of, and the distinction between, genotype and phenotype to spatial configurations ignores the possibilities of creatively manipulating materials, construction and structural systems, artifactual configurations, meanings and behavioral usage as other legitimate components of architectural process.

findings.antecedent: Professional masons and apprentices in Djenne
findings.consequent: Preservation of building/design traditions, negotiation of boundaries, injection of innovation, reinterpretation of architectural meaning
findings.quote: ...a professional association of masons, by training its apprentices, has preserved its building and design traditions. However, significantly, the apprentices have learned in the process to negotiate the boundaries of the tradition and inject innovation to generate reinterpretations of architectural meaning in local contexts.

findings.consequent: Thought embodied in form, comprising durability, utility, and the cosmos
findings.quote: W.R. Lethaby has described architecture as 'thought embodied in form,' comprising 'durability, utility, and the cosmos.'

findings.consequent: Political hierarchy, architectonics as the art of systems, rational organization of knowledge
findings.quote: When Aristotle wants to give an example of theory and practice, he quotes the 'architekton': he knows the origin of things, he is a theorist who can also teach and has at his command the labourers who are incapable of independent thought. And with that a political hierarchy is established: architectonics is defined as an art of systems, as an art therefore suitable for the rational organisation of complete branches of knowledge.

findings.consequent: Emphasis on the master builder and the product of his design and construction
findings.quote: Architecture has been frequently defined as the science (or art) of building, the word being derived from the Latin architectura. In turn this stems from the Greek arkhitekton, the combination of archos, chief, and tekton, builder, thus placing the emphasis on the master builder and the product of his design and construction.

findings.consequent: Customarily drawn from communities using structures, often owner-builder-occupiers
findings.quote: In the EVAW Oliver also stated that 'vernacular builders' (note that he does not say 'architects') are customarily drawn from the communities that use the structures, and are frequently 'owner-builder-occupiers.'

findings.consequent: Existence of specialized practitioners (e.g., Maori architect, Samoan guild of builders), contradicting the idea of everyone building
findings.quote: However, Austin concluded that the idea of traditional building being executed by everyone in a society is not correct for Oceania. His examples of more specialized practitioners included the Maori architect (tohunga), a skilled carver knowledgeable in myths and traditions, and a Samoan guild of builders (tufunga)...

findings.consequent: Terms for 'architect' (ah noah, jch'ubajel, ch'ubavil) in traditional constructions
findings.quote: A number of colonial-era Maya dictionaries also refer to the role of an 'architect' in traditional constructions. Thus, Suzanne Miles has discussed the Pokomam Maya term ah noah, or 'master architect.'... in colonial Tzotzil Maya, the term for architect is 'official builder,' jch'ubajel or ch'ubavil, or 'man who makes walls.'

findings.antecedent: Australian Aboriginal societies (pre- and early contact times)
findings.consequent: Individuals generally versed in shelter construction, with some excelling and specializing in more permanent shelter construction
findings.quote: Oliver's position on this matter appears to hold true for most Australian Aboriginal societies in pre- and early contact times, with every individual being versed in shelter construction. Nevertheless, there is anecdotal evidence to suggest that certain individuals excelled and would then specialize in more permanent shelter construction.

findings.consequent: Different sources of authority: ego-driven (capital-A architectures) vs. extra-ego/ancestral heroes/god beings (Maya and Aboriginal architectures)
findings.quote: It appears from the authors' research of Maya and Aboriginal architectures that authority referents for form-making predominantly take on extra-ego forms (ancestral heroes or god beings); this differs from capital-A architectures, where the decision-making process is clearly centered on the architect's ego-driven ability...

findings.consequent: Core sense: process(es) of cultural transmission across generations; second sense: product(s) of this process (old customs handed down); viewed as the normal process of cultural change
findings.quote: In Standard English, the term tradition has, I submit, the core sense of signifying the process(es) of the transmission or passing on of culture across the generations... Tradition has a second (metonymic) sense of signifying the product or products of this process... Tradition is no more or less than the normal process of cultural change...

findings.consequent: Minimal structure (domiciliary spaces, hearths, artifacts, windbreaks/shades), reliance on natural site qualities for comfort
findings.quote: This is a quickly made camp, comprising domiciliary spaces, hearths and artifacts, and sometimes windbreaks or shades, that is used overnight or perhaps for only a few hours... natural qualities of the chosen site are of substantial importance in enhancing residential comfort.

findings.consequent: Enhanced comfort (free-of-grass floor, good wood for cooking/warming, sound of wind) and security (sacred meanings of landscape)
findings.quote: P.W.'s preferred campsite location is in mulga woodland. He will be grumpy if there are not any mulga tree communities available... floor of the mulga forest is free of grass... Mulga is also a superior wood for cooking and warming fires... There is also a constant familiar and secure sound of wind in mulga.

findings.antecedent: Environmental properties (natural/artificial), activity spaces, behavioral rules, meanings
findings.consequent: Aboriginal Architecture (defined as selected, arranged, constructed configuration resulting in human comfort and quality of lifestyle)
findings.quote: Australian Aboriginal architecture can be defined as one that is a selected, arranged and constructed configuration of environmental properties, both natural and artificial, in and around one or more activity spaces, combined with patterns of behavioral rules and meanings, to result in human comfort and quality of lifestyle.

findings.consequent: Characterized by open spaces, sticks/grass, poles, single-cell pavilions, raised buildings, temporariness, tension/weaving, outdoor existence, ocean voyaging
findings.quote: There are clear parallels here with Austin's description of 'Pacific Architecture' as an architecture of spaces open to the sky rather than closed rooms, or sticks and grass as against mud and stones, poles as against walls, of single cell pavilions rather than labyrinthine complexes, of buildings raised in the air on stilts rather than sunk in the ground, of temporariness as against permanence, tension and weaving rather than compression and building, an outdoor existence and ocean voyaging as against a life grounded in the land.

findings.consequent: Utilization of 'space as walls' and organization using 'semiotic strategies' (signs and laws) in relation to 'centers'
findings.quote: Bob Hodge for instance, has acknowledged that Aboriginal residential camps utilize 'space as walls,' and are organized using 'semiotic strategies,' which he defines as 'signs and laws' in relation to 'centers.'

findings.consequent: Dominance of visual properties
findings.source: p. 8, citing Nalbantoglu and Wong Chong Thai
findings.quote: Gulsum Nalbantoglu and Wong Chong Thai, who challenge the primacy of visual properties, which they claim dominate contemporary architectural studies.

findings.consequent: Classification according to tectonic languages (weaving/binding) and form/space relations
findings.quote: For example, Fowler has classified Melanesian traditional architecture according to tectonic languages (weaving and binding) as well as form/space relations.

findings.antecedent: Standing behavior pattern, context (milieu), interacting persons, things, time, environment
findings.consequent: Formation of a 'behavior setting' (ecological unit with synomorphic relationship)
findings.quote: According to Roger Barker and Herbert Wright, certain attributes of people-environment interaction... combine in a complex way to form a special class of places known as 'behavior settings.' The behavior setting is 'a standing behavior pattern together with the context of this behavior, including the part of the milieu to which the behavior is attached and with which it has [a] synomorphic relationship.'

findings.consequent: Maintenance of structural qualities independently of personality; coercion of individual behavior to conform to recognized models
findings.quote: Thus the structural qualities of the setting are maintained independently of personality... Such settings involve forces which coerce individual behavior to conform to recognized models of what is correct under the circumstances.

findings.consequent: Variation with culture in how they are marked and by whom they are penetrated
findings.quote: However, according to Rapoport, the 'boundaries of [the] milieu, how they are marked, by whom they are penetrated, and so on, vary with culture.'

findings.antecedent: Selection of environmental properties and articulation of setting space with artifacts, structures, meanings
findings.consequent: Designed settings
findings.quote: Settings are designed through the selection of particular environmental properties and the articulation of the setting space with artifacts, structures and meanings.

findings.consequent: Architecture (defined as composed of these elements, where meanings are a function of activities, and activities a function of settings)
findings.quote: In relating settings to architecture, Rapoport has stated that 'architecture' is composed of activities, settings and meanings, with these three elements interwoven, whereby 'meanings' are a function of 'activities,' and 'activities' are a function of 'settings.'

findings.consequent: Consists of fixed-feature (buildings, floors, walls), semi-fixed-feature (furnishings), and non-fixed-feature (people, activities) elements
findings.quote: In an adaptation of Hall's proxemics theory, Rapoport also proposed a theory of the built environment as 'consisting of fixed-feature elements (buildings, floors, walls, etc.), semi-fixed-feature elements ('furnishings,' interior and exterior of all sorts), and non-fixed-feature elements (people and their activities and behaviors).'

findings.antecedent: Activities, settings, meanings of people, varying permanency (fixed, semi, nonfixed elements), local context, buildings, human spatial behaviors
findings.consequent: Architecture (defined as configuration facilitating high congruence between human needs and environmental attributes)
findings.quote: We agree that any definition of 'architecture' should incorporate the activities, settings and meanings of people, in conjunction with the varying degrees of permanency i.e., fixed, semi-, and nonfixed elements of the built fabric specific to its local context.

findings.consequent: Rich meanings and symbolism (sacred, ritual, ancestral, body metaphors)
findings.quote: For example, a range of semiotic references have been recorded in the ethnographic literature on Australian Aboriginal ethno-architecture.

findings.consequent: Threefold categorization: 'High-level' (cosmologies, worldviews, sacred), 'Middle-level' (identity, status, wealth, power), 'Low-level' (everyday, instrumental, mnemonic cues)
findings.quote: Rapoport also provided a threefold categorization of meanings. 'High-level' meanings relate to cosmologies... 'Middle-level' meanings are those communicating identity, status, wealth, and power... 'Low-level' everyday and instrumental meanings comprise mnemonic cues...

findings.consequent: Practical functioning of environment for users, visitors, and uninitiated
findings.quote: Rapoport explained that low-level meanings must always be present if the environment is to work in a practical manner for users, visitors, and those uninitiated into the higher levels of meaning.

findings.consequent: Knowledge by a minority; cross-cultural variation in extent of use
findings.quote: In many cultures only a minority may know the higher-level meanings of the environment... The extent of use of high- and middle-level meanings will also vary cross-culturally.

findings.antecedent: Traditional Maya dwellings (linked to cosmology/philosophy) vs. Euro-American style concrete cottages (linked to status/security)
findings.consequent: Shift in high-level meaning from cosmology/philosophy to status/security due to cultural change
findings.quote: The construction of traditional Maya dwellings in Guatemala, Belize and Mexico has always been intimately linked to elements of Maya cosmology and socio-religious philosophy. However, in contemporary Maya settlements, Euro-American-style cottages constructed of concrete and galvanized iron are proliferating through processes of both directed (imposed) and voluntary cultural change.

findings.consequent: Overlay of historical symbolism (numerological cosmology of structure spacing) onto contemporary cinder-block houses
findings.quote: During fieldwork, Davidson found a limited number of cases where certain individuals overlaid their contemporary cinder-block houses with historical symbolism (numerological cosmology of structure spacing).

findings.consequent: Possession of 'ritual attractors' (preeminent structural elements like post, ladder, ridge-pole, hearth) as high-level meaning, representing the house as a whole
findings.quote: He noted that most Austronesian homes possessed what he called a 'ritual attractor,' or a preeminent structural element of the house's architecture. This is usually a focus of ritual or at least acknowledged in ritual, and generally recognized as such from the time of construction. It represents the house as a whole in a concentrated or symbolic form.

findings.antecedent: Forked-post and cross-pole components in Arnhem Land/Cape York (Fantin's study)
findings.consequent: Function as 'ritual attractors'
findings.quote: In a separate study from northern Australia, Shaneen Fantin has elicited evidence for the symbolism of the archetypal forked-post and cross-pole in Arnhem Land and Cape York, indicating that these components were also 'ritual attractors.'

findings.antecedent: Yolngu ceremony (synthesis of song, dance, ground sculptures, ceremonial artifacts, shelters)
findings.consequent: Temporary religious architecture imbued with ancestral presence/power and ancestral aesthetic qualities
findings.quote: A creative synthesis of song, dance, ground sculptures, ceremonial artifacts and shelters thus becomes imbued with ancestral presence and power, and constitutes a temporary Yolngu religious architecture which contains ancestral aesthetic qualities.

findings.consequent: Removal or erasure of traces after performances to safeguard perceived potency
findings.quote: It is significant that this ceremonial architecture is constructed of semi-fixed and unfixed features, since all traces of it are usually removed or erased after performances to safeguard its perceived potency (FIG.5).

findings.consequent: Production of theory and concepts 'more in tune with human behaviours and actions' and deepening of environmental experience
findings.quote: In seeking to construct a cross-cultural theory of architecture that places 'meaning' at a high premium, it also seems sensible to draw on phenomenology, which is preoccupied with producing theory 'and concepts of human science which are more in tune with human behaviours and actions as they happen and exist in the world of human experience.'

findings.consequent: Tendency to always try to be 'at home' in a place, regardless of poor conditions
findings.quote: Phenomenology has shown that people always try to be at home in a place, regardless of how poor conditions might seem to the outsider.

findings.consequent: Includes surroundings, artifacts, gestures, behaviors, events, and meanings; linked to 'dwelling' which joins people with environment across time
findings.quote: A potential of phenomenology is thus to explore and describe what Husserl has called the 'life-world,' the everyday world of taken-for-grantedness, which includes surroundings, artifacts, gestures, behaviors, events and meanings. Underlying this focus on life-worlds is the wider concept of 'dwelling,' which joins people with environment and provides a link across time.

findings.consequent: Two competing theoretical paradigms: atomistic (bounded entity, defined properties) vs. interpretive (continually reinterpreted process)
findings.quote: A closer examination of the literature reveals two competing theoretical paradigms of what tradition is as a scientific construct.

findings.consequent: Tradition is continually reinterpreted; what is new can take on symbolic value as 'traditional' in reference to what is perceived as 'old'
findings.source: p. 12, citing Shils and Handler & Linnekin
findings.quote: According to Shils, unchanging traditional societies have never existed. And since all cultures change regularly, there can only be what is new - although, as Handler and Linnekin have argued, what is new can take on symbolic value as 'traditional' in reference to what is perceived as being 'old.'

findings.consequent: Appropriation by Samoans within Polynesian intellectual terms, resulting in local idealized versions of Christian spirituality
findings.quote: Refiti pointed out that this was accomplished within the intellectual terms of the Polynesians, with neither a comprehensive understanding of the Christian culture nor an attempt to authentically create a facsimile Christian religion. Only particular Christian ideas were selected and integrated with the local belief system, as these churches became local idealized versions of Christian spirituality.

findings.antecedent: New Zealand European architect's attempt to reflect Pacific identity
findings.consequent: 'Pacific architecture' as a fantasy of Pacific/European missionary paradise
findings.quote: 'Pacific architecture, is a New Zealand European architect's fantasy of what a Pacific heavenly paradise might be, based on a Pacific fantasy on what a European missionary paradise might be,' he wrote.

findings.consequent: Stereotyping (Meeting House/Marae) and perception of acculturation as loss of indigenous identity
findings.quote: He examined the stereotyping of Maori architecture by Anglo New Zealanders through the media of politics, museums and texts into a single genotype, that of the Meeting House, or 'Marae.' Any post-contact architectural acculturation by Maori was seen by the colonists to represent a loss of indigenous identity and to be somehow nonauthentic.

findings.consequent: Distinct New Zealand bicultural expression, not assimilation
findings.quote: However, McKay provided examples of the mixing of 'Pakeha' (European) and Maori motifs by Maori builder-architects as a distinctly New Zealand form of bicultural expression, and certainly not as an outcome of assimilation.

findings.antecedent: Technological power of a new medium (e.g., printing press, computer)
findings.consequent: Far-reaching global impacts and large-scale changes of tradition ('hyper-traditions')
findings.quote: It is the technological power of a new medium (e.g., the printing press or the computer) that can result in far-reaching global impacts and changes of tradition at an unusually large scale. Perhaps it would be appropriate to apply the term 'hyper-traditions' to this category of cultural change (FIG.7).

findings.consequent: Dynamic societies, in a continual process of adaptation, choice, and constraint
findings.quote: As Anderson wrote, indigenous cultures are 'dynamic societies, in a continual process of adaptation, choice, and constraint.'

findings.consequent: Temporal properties including articulation with activity (time, frequency, duration), internal transformation during place-bound activity, mental association of beliefs/values/meanings, and externally imposed changes
findings.quote: The types of change associated with architectural settings include their articulation with activity (involves a time, frequency and duration of usage); their internal transformation during periods of characteristic place-bound activity; the mental association of beliefs, values, names, and other meanings with them (a mental change which does not necessarily occur at the place under focus); and externally imposed changes to them (directed cultural changes, natural catastrophes).

findings.antecedent: Internal forces controlling setting form (Memmott's observation)
findings.consequent: Constancy of setting/architectural character, with repetitive internal change, due to stabilizing/equilibrating effects
findings.quote: However, as Memmott has noted, a constancy of setting or architectural character is often maintained, together with repetitive internal change, due to the stabilizing or equilibrating effects of the internal forces which control setting form.

findings.consequent: Integration of natural time orders (cyclic changes from environmental rhythms, climate, flora, fauna, lunar, animal behavior), significant role in hunter-gatherer traditions, influence on movement, campsite selection, shelter form, lifestyle, and emphasis on social quality of events
findings.quote: Indigenous constructs of time tend to integrate natural time orders which are dynamic in their own right, displaying cyclic changes of properties caused by natural environmental rhythms (solar rhythms and associated diurnal/nocturnal rhythms, seasonal cycles, changes in climate, flora, fauna, lunar rhythms, and associated tidal movement and animal behavior).

findings.consequent: No abstract units of time/space to measure distance, no quantified geometry/chronology, scale less important than sequential correctness/causal links, corresponds to topological concept of space
findings.quote: There are then no abstract units of time and space that indigenous people use to measure distance between events, i.e., no quantified geometry of space or chronology of time. The overall result is the possibility of expanding or compressing time and/or space in historical and geographical thought. Scale is thus less important than the sequential correctness of events in space and time, and the nature of causal links between them. Such concepts of space and time correspond closely to the topological concept of space.

findings.antecedent: Maori space and time construct (McKay's description)
findings.consequent: More like a constellation, with past/people of past always felt in the present, intermeshing, surrounding, forming interpretable patterns
findings.quote: ...the Maori space and time construct can be thought of more like a constellation with the past and the people of the past always felt in the present, like the constellations of the sky - enmeshing, surrounding - always before you, always behind, forming patterns that can be interpreted in various ways.

findings.consequent: Sense of Ancestral Beings' active presence, linking ancient past to present
findings.quote: Similarly, in the case of Aboriginal elder P.W. in his 'traveling camp' presented earlier, there is a sense of the presence of Ancestral Beings from the Dreamtime having an active presence at the campsite, linking the ancient past to the present.

findings.consequent: Disruption of traditional Indigenous structures, but also transformation and prevalence in contemporary situations, with experiences based on multiple cultural constructs
findings.quote: The imposition of Western space and time structures and concepts has disrupted traditional Indigenous structures. Nevertheless, in many cases those traditional structures have been transformed and may well prevail in contemporary situations. Contemporary experiences of space and time in relation to architecture and place are often based upon multiple cultural constructs.

findings.consequent: Classification of all environmental types under environmental design, subsuming cultural landscapes (sacred sites created by ancestral heroes)
findings.quote: Rapoport has classified all such environmental types under the category of environmental design, which he subsumes within his Environment-Behavior Studies (EBS) approach. Rapoport also included cultural landscapes, which in the case of Aboriginal Australia would consist of sacred sites believed to have been created by both stationary and traveling ancestral heroes...

findings.consequent: Criticized as 'extremely deterministic' and 'eliminating the agency of the individual member of society, leaving little if any room for improvisation and innovation'
findings.quote: Rapoport's theory has been criticized as being 'extremely deterministic and [eliminating] the agency of the individual member of society, leaving little if any room for improvisation and innovation.'

findings.consequent: Inclusion in a comprehensive theory of architecture, covering habitat building and socio-semantic elaboration
findings.quote: We also converge with Egenter in that animal architecture needs to be included, covering topics such as habitat building and the socio-semantic elaboration of such.

findings.antecedent: McBride's general theory of social organization/behavior (all animals, including humans)
findings.consequent: Application to people-environment interaction (attention, perception, behavior, social process) and therapeutic architectural design for institutional settings
findings.quote: Based on his earlier empirical research on chickens and pigs, he engaged in the construction of a general theory of social organization and behavior that applied to all animals, including humans. His later work then moved to the specific application of this theory to people-environment interaction (attention, perception, behavior and social process) and the challenge of therapeutic architectural design for institutional settings.

limitations: It has been beyond the scope of this article to execute such a program of analysis; the authors have merely begun to sketch out some of the central topics (p. 15).

One of the ongoing theoretical tasks is how all environmental types and productions may be classified under such a revised definition of architecture and be distinguished and sorted into subcategories that are useful in understanding their design properties and values (p. 16).

Rapoport's theory, which is drawn upon, has been criticized as 'extremely deterministic and [eliminating] the agency of the individual member of society, leaving little if any room for improvisation and innovation' (p. 16).
minimum_safe_summary: This theoretical article proposes a cross-cultural theory of architecture to encompass all human behavior related to built environments, challenging the Euro-American 'capital-A architecture' concept for its historical exclusion of indigenous traditions. Key findings include the dynamic nature of 'tradition' as cultural transmission and change, the importance of 'behavior settings' (activities, context, synomorphic relationship) as a form of architecture, and the multi-layered nature of meaning (ideological, social, behavioral) in built forms, which varies cross-culturally and shifts over time. The authors acknowledge that fully executing such a comprehensive analysis is beyond the scope of this initial article, which primarily sketches central topics for future development, and that existing theories, while useful, have faced critiques regarding determinism and the agency of individuals.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: A unifying cross-cultural theoretical framework of architecture
